source.title: Mitigating sensitive information leakage in LLMs4Code through machine unlearning
source.authors: Shan-Zhi Gu; Zhao-Yang Qu; Ruotong Geng; Ming-Yang Geng; Shangwen Wang; Chuan-Fu Xu; Haotian Wang; Zhipeng Lin; Dezun Dong

record.file_problem: The paper text is present through its figures and references. The page labels extend to Page 20 of 14, but the text is readable and not visibly cut off.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates post-unlearning sensitive-information leakage and retained code-generation performance using its own privacy benchmark, rather than testing the recovery attacks named in the claim.
record.gate_note: The study tests direct privacy queries after unlearning, but does not test whether the listed recovery attacks restore forgotten knowledge. Table 2 describes categories of privacy-protecting outputs; it is not a recovery-attack evaluation. Table 3 reports the proportions of observed leakage classified as direct or indirect, rather than attack-based recovery.
record.test_reason: Applies GA, GA+GD and GA+KL to eight code LLMs and measures post-unlearning leak rate on held-out forget-set queries plus Pass@1 utility. This bears on version A's efficacy and utility part in a new setting (code models, privacy data). No recovery attack is run, so B–F are untested.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that GA-based unlearning substantially reduces sensitive-information leakage in code LLMs with little loss of code-generation ability, and that GA+GD works best. They also find a shift toward indirect leakage that future methods must address. Their headline figures are inconsistent: over 50%, up to 72%, and about 80% reduction. The abstract names three models although Table 1 covers eight.
record.recipe_differences: Tests forget-set GA, GA+GD, and GA+KL on synthetic code-completion privacy data, with leak rate and Pass@1 measures. It does not implement or test the recovery attacks named in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: Leak-rate outcomes vary by model and unlearning method. The authors report GA+GD as generally yielding the lowest leak rates; Table 1 shows method-specific differences.

fits_no_version.finding: Among leak cases after unlearning, the share of indirect leakage (non-queried attributes) rises and the direct share falls, across all models and methods (Table 3). The ratios are conditional on leak cases.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning suppresses the queried sensitive value but shifts residual leakage toward contextually related, non-queried attributes.

record.problems: The forget set is synthetic and generated for this study; the authors note that it may not represent real-world code scenarios. Leakage judgments rely on manual assessment by five experts, and the authors acknowledge possible subjectivity. The authors also note that their prompts may not cover the space of adversarial queries. No uncertainty estimates are reported.
record.rows_left_out: The 60-row limit was reached. Table 3 rows for GA and GA+KL across models were omitted, along with some Table 3 ratios for models beyond the first five listed; Table 3 contains additional direct and indirect ratios for CodeQwen-3B, CodeQwen-7B, and CodeQwen-14B and for the other unlearning methods. Table 1 Pass@1 results for methods other than GA+GD were not separately extracted. Table 1, Table 3, Section 4.1, and Section 4.3.

untested.parts: Whether simple attacks recover the knowledge. Only the study's own direct code-completion prompts are used; the authors say these may not exhaust adversarial queries. No chance or floor level is defined. Utility is code Pass@1 only.
Entire version: no relearning or fine-tuning attack.
Entire version: no activation ablation or representation analysis.
Entire version: no rephrasing, jailbreak, multilingual or in-context attack.
Entire version: no attack-robust method proposed or tested.

missing.what: Pass@1 after GA and GA+KL for all eight models. Examples: AIXCoder GA+KL 55.0 vs 60.0; CodeQwen-7B GA 65.0 vs 71.1; CodeLlama-34B GA+KL 72.0 vs 75.8.
Fine-grained leakage by attribute type (email, password, address, bank balance) per method; KL leaves more address/password leakage.

record.verdict_notes: Important caveat for A: the paper never states that the fictional forget-set profiles were trained into the models before unlearning. Zero-shot 'leaks' of fictional people's data may therefore be hallucinated or prompt-derived values rather than memorized knowledge. Unlearning is done on 90% of queries and evaluated on a held-out 10%. Leak judgments are manual by five experts, and no uncertainty is reported. Without any attack, the study cannot speak to shallow versus deep unlearning; its results bear only on surface efficacy under direct queries. Code-generation models are a new setting, hence T3.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not assess whether leakage reaches chance, define a chance level, or test post-unlearning recovery attacks. Pass@1 measures code-generation utility, not general language ability.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning or relearning attack is tested.
No activation direction is ablated and no analysis tests whether unlearning blocks access rather than deleting knowledge.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, language variation, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
The study does not propose or test a method claimed to resist the listed recovery attacks.

relationships.condition: CodeLlama-7B/13B/34B and CodeQwen-7B/14B under GA+GD, direct-query evaluation only
relationships.reason: Leak rate falls about 78–85% (e.g. 32.7→5.0) while Pass@1 drops at most 3.5 points (r7, r11, r15, r27, r31, r34, r35, r36, r39, r40).
relationships.display_finding: Direct-query leakage fell by about 78–85%, including a decline from 32.7 to 5.0, while Pass@1 dropped by at most 3.5 points.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: CodeLlama-7B/13B/34B and CodeQwen-7B/14B under GA+GD, direct-query evaluation only
source_check.reason: GA+GD cuts leak rate 78-85% (e.g. CodeLlama-34B 32.7 to 5.0; CodeQwen-14B 26.2 to 4.7), and Pass@1 drops 0.5-3.5 points (r7, r11, r15, r27, r31, r34-r36, r39, r40). The metric counts any leak, direct or indirect, on 500 forget-set test queries. No recovery attack is run.

relationships.reason: Leakage only falls to 10.4–15.9% from 23.2% and GA+GD costs 3 Pass@1 points; unlearning is far from complete (r2, r3, r4, r33).
relationships.display_finding: AIXCoder leakage fell from 23.2% to 10.4–15.9%, while GA+GD reduced Pass@1 by 3 points.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Leak rate falls only from 23.2 to 15.9 (GA), 13.1 (GA+GD) and 10.4 (GA+KL), a 31-55% cut. Pass@1 drops from 60.0 to 57.0 under GA+GD and to 55.0 under GA+KL (r2-r4, r33).

relationships.condition: Smaller CodeQwen models (1.5B, 3B) and GA/GA+KL variants generally
relationships.reason: Residual leak rates of 6.8–9.5% remain; reductions are about 50–67% rather than near-complete (r18–r24). Per the text, GA+KL costs up to 5 Pass@1 points and GA costs 6.1 on CodeQwen-7B.
relationships.display_finding: CodeQwen-1.5B/3B retained leakage of 6.8–9.5% after reductions of 47–67%; GA on CodeQwen-7B reduced Pass@1 from 71.1 to 65.0.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Smaller CodeQwen models (1.5B, 3B) and GA/GA+KL variants generally
source_check.reason: The label fits only CodeQwen-1.5B/3B (r18-r20, r22-r24): 47-67% cuts with 6.8-9.5% residual leak. 'GA/GA+KL generally' does not fit. r28 (CodeQwen-7B GA+KL, 23.3 to 5.0, 78.5%) beats GA+GD and costs only 1.3 Pass@1. CodeLlama and CodeQwen-14B GA/GA+KL cut 69-81%. The 'up to 5 Pass@1 points' for GA+KL is AIXCoder (l1's group); CodeQwen GA+KL costs 1.3-3.3. Narrow to CodeQwen-1.5B/3B, plus CodeQwen-7B GA's 6.1-point Pass@1 cost (71.1 to 65.0).

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

relation.reason: Measures post-unlearning leak rate and Pass@1, which bears on A's efficacy and utility parts. It runs no recovery attack, so B-F are untested.

tranche.reason: New setting (code LLMs, synthetic privacy data, GA/GA+GD/GA+KL) with efficacy and utility results bearing on version A. It is not the same method or measure as WMDP/RMU, so T3 fits better than T2.

source_check.notes: Leak rate is human-judged on 500 forget-set test queries and counts direct and indirect leaks. Table 3 gives shares of leak cases, so absolute indirect leakage still falls (e.g. CodeLlama-34B about 15.4% to 3.3% under GA+GD). The text never says the models are instruct variants. l0 rows are 'partial' (residual 4.7-5.6% leak) under a supports verdict. The authors' claim that GA+GD is 'consistently lowest' fails for AIXCoder and CodeQwen-7B, where GA+KL is lower. No attacks are run, so B-F are untested.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: All tested models and unlearning methods in Table 1
reader_labels.reason: Leak rates decline but remain above zero after unlearning, and the study gives no chance benchmark; the recovery-attack component is untested. GA+GD Pass@1 is generally close to baseline but falls by 3.5 points for CodeQwen-7B. Rows r2-r4, r6-r8, r10-r12, r14-r16, r18-r20, r22-r24, r26-r28, r30-r32, r33-r40.
